\documentclass{article}
\usepackage{amsmath}
\usepackage{amssymb}
\title{A Note on Price Dynamics with Sticky Adjustment}
\author{Working Paper Draft}
\date{May 2026}
\begin{document}
\maketitle
\section{Setup}
Let the consumption bundle be $x \in \mathbb{R}^n_{+}$, where $n$ denotes the number of goods.
Preferences are represented by a continuous utility function $u : \mathbb{R}^n_{+} \to \mathbb{R}$.
The budget set collects all bundles whose cost does not exceed wealth.
Prices are strictly positive, and wealth $w$ is fixed throughout.
Demand is the bundle that maximizes utility subject to the budget constraint.
We assume strict convexity so that demand is single valued.
Income effects are allowed to be nonzero for every good.
The indirect utility function inherits continuity from the primitives.
Roy's identity recovers demand from indirect utility.
These regularity conditions are standard in the literature.
They hold for most parametric families used in applied work.
We flag explicitly whenever an argument needs more structure.
\section{Adjustment}
Firms update prices sluggishly in response to excess demand.
The adjustment speed is common across markets.
Excess demand is continuous in prices by the maximum theorem.
The cost function $c : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ maps output into total cost.
Marginal cost is the derivative of $c$ wherever it exists.
Fixed costs shift $c$ vertically without changing its slope.
We rule out corner solutions by an interiority assumption.
Adjustment costs are quadratic in the size of the price change.
This functional form keeps the first-order conditions tractable.
It also matches the calibration targets reported in the appendix.
The steady state coincides with the Walrasian equilibrium.
Local stability follows from a standard Lyapunov argument.
\section{Examples}
A Cobb-Douglas example illustrates the main mechanism.
With two goods, the adjustment path is a spiral toward equilibrium.
A Leontief example shows that complementarities slow convergence.
Numerical simulations confirm the qualitative predictions.
The half-life of adjustment rises with the share of complementary goods.
Welfare losses are convex in the adjustment speed.
Small menu costs generate sizable real effects.
The quantitative results are robust to the simulation horizon.
We report sensitivity checks for the discount rate.
The appendix collects the longer proofs.
\section{Welfare}
The welfare cost of stickiness is measured in equivalent variation.
Consumers bear most of the burden when demand is elastic.
Producers absorb the loss when demand is steep.
The distribution of losses tracks the expenditure shares.
Poorer households spend a larger share on sticky-price goods.
This makes the welfare cost mildly regressive.
Transfers financed by a lump-sum tax can offset the regressivity.
The required transfers are modest in the calibrated economy.
We report the decomposition for three preference specifications.
The ranking of policies is stable across specifications.
\section{Discussion}
The results connect the menu-cost literature with welfare analysis.
Earlier work focused on the positive side of price rigidity.
Our decomposition makes the normative side explicit.
The framework extends to multi-sector economies.
Sectoral heterogeneity in adjustment speeds amplifies the losses.
Input-output linkages propagate the distortion upstream.
These extensions are left for future work.
The current draft keeps the focus on the one-sector case.
Preliminary results for two sectors look similar.
Comments from seminar audiences shaped this version.
\end{document}
